name: AI2 Reasoning Challenge (ARC)
description: A dataset of 7,787 natural, non-diagram, multiple-choice grade-school science questions authored for standardized human tests, partitioned into a Challenge Set and an Easy Set, along with the ARC Corpus of 14M science-related sentences and baseline models for question answering.
creator: Peter Clark, Isaac Cowhey, Oren Etzioni, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal, Carissa Schoenick, Oyvind Tafjord
citeAs: Peter Clark, Isaac Cowhey, Oren Etzioni, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal, Carissa Schoenick, Oyvind Tafjord. Think you have Solved Question Answering? Try ARC, the AI2 Reasoning Challenge. arXiv:1803.05457v1, 2018.
rai:dataCollection: The ARC dataset was assembled through several months of extensive search and investigation to obtain publicly releasable natural science questions authored for standardized tests. The dataset consists of 7,787 non-diagram, multiple-choice science questions drawn from a variety of sources, including state assessment programs, NAEP, TIMSS, and an anonymous content partner. The dataset was partitioned into a Challenge Set and an Easy Set based on whether two baseline solvers, an information retrieval solver and a PMI solver, answered the questions incorrectly or not. In addition, the ARC Corpus was created by mining science-related sentences from the Web using a major search engine and automatically constructed queries from about 100 hand-written templates for 80 science topics, collecting top documents, de-duplicating them, stripping content to text, chunking into sentences, and augmenting with the AristoMini corpus.
rai:dataCollectionType: Document analysis, Web Scraping, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data sources for the question set were standardized test questions from sources such as ACTAAP, AIMS, Alaska Department of Education & Early Development, California Standards Test, FCAT, Louisiana Department of Education, Maryland School Assessment, MCAS, Maine Educational Assessment, Michigan Educational Assessment Program, an anonymous AI2 content partner ('Mercury'), NAEP, NC READY, New York Regents, Ohio Achievement Tests, TAKS, TIMSS, Virginia Standards of Learning, and WASL. Raw data for the ARC Corpus came from Web documents retrieved via a major search engine using automatically instantiated science-topic query templates, and was augmented with the AristoMini corpus containing Wiktionary definitions, Simple Wikipedia science articles, and additional science sentences collected from the Web.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Questions were sorted into a Challenge Set of 2,590 questions and an Easy Set of 5,197 questions. A Challenge question was operationally defined as one answered incorrectly by both an IR solver and a PMI solver. The ARC Corpus documents were collected, de-duplicated, stripped down to text, and chunked into sentences; the corpus was then augmented with AristoMini.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For the question set, only non-diagram, multiple-choice science questions were included. For the ARC Corpus, queries were automatically constructed from hand-written templates and science-topic term lists; top documents from search results were collected and de-duplicated; document content was stripped to capture just the text; and the resulting text was chunked into sentences. In entailment-based baselines, retrieved sentences were filtered to remove long sentences (>300 characters), sentences with negation, and noisy sentences.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The questions themselves were authored for human standardized tests. No new human annotation process for labeling dataset items is described for ARC. The only described labeling-like process is the automatic partitioning of questions into Challenge and Easy sets based on whether two baseline solvers answered them incorrectly. The paper also mentions that the Science Entailment dataset used to train some baseline models had premises and hypotheses annotated by crowdworkers as entailing or not, but this is not described as annotation of ARC itself.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper notes that categorization of knowledge and reasoning types in sampled ARC questions is approximate and requires subjective judgment about the main challenge exhibited by different questions.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Elasticsearch was used in the IR-based filtering and retrieval pipeline; Open IE was used to extract structured representations for DGEM and DGEM-OpenIE; a proprietary parser and chunker were also used for DGEM.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The ARC Dataset, Corpus, three baseline neural models, and leaderboard are available at http://data.allenai.org/arc. The paper states that for up-to-date results users should see the ARC leaderboard, and invites the community to submit new entries via the ARC website. No explicit versioning schedule or deprecation policy is described.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Question grade level is included, ranging from 3rd grade to 9th grade, corresponding to students typically of age 8 through 13 years.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to encourage AI research on more advanced question answering requiring reasoning and commonsense, rather than surface-level retrieval. The authors present ARC as a challenge to the community and argue that progress on ARC would be a significant step forward for AI research.
rai:dataBiases: The paper discusses that many prior QA datasets are biased toward retrieval-style questions solvable by surface-level cues, and that standardized-test datasets can have scores dominated by simple algorithms, biasing research toward incremental improvements in retrieval and statistical correlation methods. ARC addresses this by creating a Challenge partition filtered to exclude questions solvable by simple IR and co-occurrence methods. The paper also notes that nearly all non-IR solvers depend on simple IR retrieval, whose bias is toward sentences very similar to the question and away from sentences that only partially match but together explain the answer.
rai:dataLimitations: The operational definition of a Challenge question only approximates the informal goal of being a hard question. The categorization of knowledge and reasoning types is approximate and subjective. The ARC Corpus contains indirect mentions of relevant knowledge, and exploiting them is not trivial; the corpus does not solve the challenge of correctly identifying and reasoning with this knowledge or injecting unstated commonsense knowledge. The baseline entailment conversion from questions to assertions can produce ungrammatical sentences, and a more sophisticated rule-based approach was left to future work. The corpus relevance analysis was based on informal sampled analyses.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for advanced question answering research and benchmarking. It includes train/dev/test partitions for both Challenge and Easy sets. The ARC Corpus is released as an optional supporting corpus for systems tackling the challenge, and systems are not restricted to using it. Baseline models are provided to help the community get started, and the leaderboard supports evaluation and submission of new entries.
